claim: For the exponential localization ansatz used by Li and Wang in arXiv:quant-ph/0403178, the average-concurrence estimate cannot have the quadratic localization-length dependence \(\langle C\rangle\propto\xi^2/M\) printed in their Eq. (8) once the wavefunction is normalized. With lattice spacing one, the normalized continuum profile \(\psi(x)=\xi^{-1/2}e^{-|x|/\xi}\) gives the source's own one-localization-length truncation \(\langle C\rangle_{\rm trunc}=[4(1-e^{-1})^2\xi-1]/M\), and the full profile gives \([4\xi-1]/M\). For the exact normalized finite-chain profile \(\psi_n=Z_L^{-1/2}r^{|n|}\), \(r=e^{-1/\xi}\), \(-L\le n\le L\), the concurrence mass \(K_L=M\bar C_L\) equals \(S_L^2/Z_L-1\), where \(S_L=1+2r(1-r^L)/(1-r)\) and \(Z_L=1+2r^2(1-r^{2L})/(1-r^2)\). Sending the boundaries away at fixed \(\xi\) gives \(K_\infty=2r(r^2+r+2)/[(1-r)(1+r^2)]=4\xi-1-2/(3\xi)+59/(180\xi^3)+O(\xi^{-5})\). Thus the source's quadratic scaling is a normalization artifact; within its exponential-profile model the leading dependence is linear in \(\xi\). This does not assert an exact universal law for arbitrary Anderson eigenstates, and the qualitative conclusion that stronger localization lowers the average concurrence may still hold.

scientific_limitations: The result corrects the scaling inference from an exponential-envelope ansatz; it is not a universal exact law for arbitrary Anderson eigenstates.
The continuum derivation sets lattice spacing to one and idealizes the localized state by a symmetric exponential envelope.
Finite boundaries and amplitude fluctuations can change finite-system quantitative behavior.
title: Normalization removes the quadratic localization-length law for average concurrence
